lesson.title: Turning Observations Into Evidence: Data Collection
lesson.summary: Data collection is the disciplined process of recording measurements and observations during an experiment in a way that is complete, honest, and organized enough to actually test a hypothesis.
lesson.body:
The scientific method only works if the hypothesis testing step produces something usable afterward, and that something is data. Data collection is the process of systematically recording measurements and observations while an experiment is underway, and it draws directly on the Measurement unit, since most data in chemistry consists of numerical measurements: masses, volumes, temperatures, times, and concentrations, each recorded with appropriate units and a sensible number of significant figures. Good data collection is not just about writing numbers down, it is about writing down the right numbers, at the right time, in a way that someone else, or you later, can understand and trust.

Chemists distinguish between two broad categories of data. Quantitative data consists of numerical measurements, such as recording that a reaction reached 78 degrees Celsius or that 25.0 mL of solution was used. Qualitative data consists of descriptive observations that cannot be reduced to a number, such as noting that a solution turned from clear to deep blue, that a precipitate formed as a fine white powder, or that a reaction released a sharp, vinegar like odor. Both types matter: qualitative observations often reveal that a reaction occurred at all, while quantitative data lets you calculate exact quantities, rates, or yields once you know a reaction happened.

A well kept lab notebook reflects habits that separate reliable data from unreliable data. Every measurement should be recorded immediately, at the moment it is taken, rather than reconstructed from memory afterward, since memory of an exact reading fades within minutes. Every value needs its unit attached at the moment of recording, since a number like 25.0 without mL, g, or degrees Celsius becomes meaningless once context is lost. Unexpected results should be recorded exactly as observed, not adjusted toward what the experimenter expected to see, because a surprising result is often the most scientifically interesting part of an experiment. If a value looks like a mistake, the original number should be crossed out with a single legible line rather than erased, with the corrected value written beside it, so the record of what actually happened is preserved.

Repetition is another core principle of sound data collection. A single trial could be thrown off by an unnoticed error, a contaminated sample, or ordinary random fluctuation, so chemists typically repeat a measurement multiple times and record every trial individually rather than just a final average. For example, if a student measures the volume of gas produced across three trials and gets 42.1 mL, 41.8 mL, and 42.3 mL, recording all three values, rather than only their average of 42.1 mL, preserves information about how consistent the results were, which connects directly to judging precision. Organizing this data into a clearly labeled table, with columns for trial number, measured quantity, and units, makes patterns and outliers far easier to spot than a disorganized list of numbers.

Careful, honest data collection is what makes the rest of the scientific process possible. A brilliant hypothesis and a well designed experiment are wasted if the resulting data is incomplete, mislabeled, or quietly cleaned up to match expectations, since any conclusion drawn afterward is only as trustworthy as the data it rests on. The next step in this unit, graphing data, depends entirely on having a complete, well organized data set to work with, since a graph can only reveal a trend the underlying data actually captured.
